passage:
A grey morning in Valencia. Rafael held up the thick red coat. “Coat on, Rosa, it's cold.”
Rosa shook her head hard, side to side, and backed against the fridge.
Rafael didn't grab her arm. He crouched. “No coat? Okay. Coat or jumper?” He held up both.
Rosa looked from one to the other, then pointed at the striped jumper and lifted her arms.
“Jumper it is,” said Rafael, and they were out of the door.

qa.q: What did Rosa back up against?
qa.a: She backed against the fridge.

qa.q: What was Rosa feeling when she shook her head at the coat?
qa.a: She was feeling cross and determined to refuse the coat, and probably wanted some control over what she wore; a head shake is her way of saying no before she has many words.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Rafael treated the head shake as real communication and offered a choice between two warm things, which respected her no and still got her dressed.

qa.q: How did Rafael feel when Rosa shook her head, judging by what he did?
qa.a: He seems patient rather than annoyed, since he crouched calmly instead of grabbing her arm.

grounding: It shows a toddler shaking her head to refuse, showing a wish for control, and a parent responding to it with respect.

passage:
In the Guwahati flat, Hafsa sat on the floor with a bowl of khichdi. Bhupen turned his head towards her, mouth open, babbling between spoonfuls.
After a few more bites he turned his head away and stared at the window.
Hafsa held the spoon near his lips. He turned further.
“All done?” she asked, and put the bowl down. “Okay, finished.”
Bhupen swung his head back and grinned, then crawled off to his blocks.

qa.q: What was in Hafsa's bowl?
qa.a: The bowl had khichdi in it.

qa.q: What does Bhupen turning his head away suggest he wanted?
qa.a: It suggests he was full or had simply had enough and wanted the meal to end; he seemed content, not upset, once she stopped.

qa.q: Why was putting the bowl down a good choice?
qa.a: It showed Bhupen that his turn-away was heard, so he learns his signals matter and meals stay pleasant.

qa.q: What would change if Hafsa kept pushing the spoon?
qa.a: Bhupen might get frustrated and fuss, and learn that turning away does not work, making meals a struggle.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler turning his head towards a caregiver to engage and away to end a feed, and the caregiver respecting it.

passage:
“Abba! Jahnavi fell off the slide!”
Imran scooped her up. Jahnavi was whimpering, shoulders jammed up by her ears, body stiff.
“Where does it hurt, jaan? Knee?” He checked it. “Just a scrape. And your arm?” She let him move it without crying.
At home, Mumma asked, “Is she still upset?”
Imran looked down. Jahnavi lay on his chest, shoulders soft and loose, fingers curled in his shirt.
“No,” he whispered. “Look. She's asleep.”

qa.q: What did Jahnavi fall off?
qa.a: Jahnavi fell off the slide.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi's loose, dropped shoulders on Imran's chest show about how she felt?
qa.a: They showed she felt safe and relaxed again, unlike the stiff, raised shoulders after the fall that suggested pain or fright.

qa.q: What did Imran do that a wise caregiver would copy?
qa.a: He treated her tense shoulders as a sign of possible pain and checked her knee and arm before comforting her.

qa.q: How might Mumma feel when she sees Jahnavi's soft shoulders?
qa.a: Mumma would likely feel relieved that Jahnavi has settled and is no longer upset.

grounding: It shows a toddler with tense shoulders after a fall and loose, dropped shoulders later in a parent's arms, a sign of safety.

passage:
The doorbell rang in the Stockholm apartment and his mother's friend Mina came in, stamping snow off her boots.
Oskar stopped playing. His shoulders crept up towards his ears and he edged behind his father's legs.
“Hello, Oskar!” said Mina, reaching out.
“He needs a minute,” said his father gently.
Mina sat down on the floor, took off her scarf and started stacking his blocks.
Oskar watched. Slowly his shoulders came down. Then he walked over and handed her a red block.

qa.q: What did Mina do after sitting down on the floor?
qa.a: She took off her scarf and started stacking his blocks.

qa.q: What was Oskar feeling when his shoulders crept up to his ears?
qa.a: He was feeling shy and uneasy with someone new, and hunching was a way of protecting himself.

qa.q: What did Mina do that helped Oskar warm up?
qa.a: She stopped reaching for him, sat at his level and played nearby, letting him come to her in his own time.

qa.q: How did Oskar's father see the moment?
qa.a: His father saw that Oskar was shy and needed time, not that he was being rude.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler hunching his shoulders when shy with a visitor and an adult letting him warm up.

subtype: Raising arms to be picked up [Expressing]
passage:
I'm Simran, and my little sister Ishita is two. In the park yesterday a big dog barked right behind her.
She spun round and stretched both arms straight up at Papa, making a little whine. She didn't say anything, but it was obvious what she wanted.
Papa picked her up at once and held her. She tucked her head under his chin.
A man on the bench said she was too big to be carried. Papa just smiled and kept holding her.

qa.q: How old is Ishita?
qa.a: Ishita is two.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she stretched her arms up at Papa?
qa.a: She was scared by the barking dog and wanted comfort and closeness; raising her arms was a clear request to be lifted.

qa.q: Why was Papa right to pick Ishita up?
qa.a: Answering her raised arms made her feel safe, which builds her trust, and asking to be carried is normal at her age.

qa.q: How does the man on the bench see Ishita being carried?
qa.a: The man thinks she is too big to be carried, not seeing that she was frightened.

grounding: It shows a toddler raising both arms to be picked up after a fright, a clear request for comfort that a parent answers.

passage:
Toddler music class note, Saturday. From Ojas, class leader.
When Zeenat's Nani came through the door at the end of class, Zeenat spread her arms wide and flapped them up and down, running in a wobbly line, shrieking.
One parent pulled her son back, worried Zeenat might hit him.
I don't think so. Her face was all smile; it was joy, lots of energy with nowhere to go.
Next time I'll make a clear space by the door for pickups.

qa.q: Who came through the door at the end of class?
qa.a: Zeenat's Nani came through the door.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when she flapped her arms and shrieked?
qa.a: She was feeling excited and happy to see her Nani; her smiling face shows joy, not anger.

qa.q: What is Ojas's plan, and why does it help?
qa.a: Ojas plans a clear space by the door at pickup, so excited children can move freely without bumping others.

qa.q: How did the other parent read Zeenat's flapping arms?
qa.a: The parent was worried Zeenat might hit her son and read the movement as a possible threat.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler spreading and flapping her arms with excitement at a favourite person, showing joy rather than aggression.

passage:
Monday. Kavitha Aunty from next door sang a clapping song on the step. Ayesha watched her hands, completely still.
Wednesday. Kavitha sang it again. Ayesha brought her palms together, missed, tried again, and made a soft pat.
Saturday. Ayesha stacked three cups by herself, looked straight at Kavitha, and clapped, grinning. Kavitha clapped too. They clapped together until Ayesha fell over laughing.

qa.q: How many cups did Ayesha stack by herself on Saturday?
qa.a: She stacked three cups by herself.

qa.q: How can you tell Ayesha was proud on Saturday?
qa.a: She looked straight at Kavitha, grinned and clapped after stacking the cups, sharing her delight at her own achievement.

qa.q: How can an adult make clapping a happy routine?
qa.a: By singing clapping songs and clapping back with the child, as Kavitha did, so it becomes something they share.

qa.q: What is it like for Kavitha when Ayesha claps at her?
qa.a: Kavitha probably feels delighted and included, since Ayesha chose her to share the moment with.

grounding: It shows a toddler learning to clap at a song and then after an achievement, sharing joy and copying an adult.

passage:
The vegetable market in Dadar was loud and packed. Mahima didi held Rehana on her hip, then set her down by a stall.
Rehana's hand shot up and clasped two of Mahima's fingers, tight.
“I'm here,” said Mahima.
A minute later Rehana let go and stretched her other arm towards a bunch of bananas, fingers opening and closing.
“You want a banana?” Mahima laughed. She broke one off, paid, and Rehana clutched it to her chest.

qa.q: Where did Mahima set Rehana down?
qa.a: She set her down by a stall.

qa.q: What did Rehana want when she clasped Mahima's fingers, and when she reached for the bananas?
qa.a: Clasping the fingers showed she wanted to feel safe and close in the noisy market; reaching for the bananas showed she wanted one, a clear, eager request.

qa.q: How did Mahima help Rehana communicate?
qa.a: She answered both gestures and put them into words, "I'm here" and "You want a banana?", which helps Rehana link reaching to meaning.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel when Rehana grabs her fingers so tightly?
qa.a: Mahima would probably feel touched and trusted, and more careful to keep Rehana close in the crowd.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler clasping a hand for closeness and reaching for an object she wants, early bonding and communication.

subtype: Beckoning and thumbs-up copied from adults [Expressing]
passage:
Crèche note, Thursday. From Swati.
Preeti has started copying grown-up gestures. She curls her fingers to say “come here” to the other children, the way her father does at pickup.
Today she dropped her cup of water, looked at me, and gave a big thumbs-up.
I didn't laugh or say “good.” I said, “Uh-oh, water fell. Let's get a cloth.” She watched my face and helped wipe.
She's copying the shapes; the meaning comes from how we answer.

qa.q: What did Preeti give Swati after dropping her cup?
qa.a: She gave a big thumbs-up.

qa.q: What was Preeti likely feeling when she gave a thumbs-up after the spill?
qa.a: She was probably curious and a bit unsure, trying out a gesture she had copied and watching to see what it meant, rather than being pleased about the spill.

qa.q: Why was Swati's response a good one?
qa.a: Swati named what really happened and did not praise the thumbs-up, so Preeti can learn what the gesture means from the response.

qa.q: What would change if Swati had laughed and said "good"?
qa.a: Preeti might learn that a thumbs-up goes with spilling things, giving the gesture the wrong meaning.

grounding: It shows a toddler copying come-here and thumbs-up gestures without full understanding, with meaning following the adult's response.

passage:
Joseph Uncle from the fourth floor stepped out of the lift in the Chennai apartment block. Karthik, on his Amma's hip, flapped his hand up and down.
“Bye-bye to you too!” laughed Joseph.
Then Karthik stretched out one finger at the window ledge and made a loud “Ah!”
Joseph bent to look. “Pigeon! That's a pigeon.”
Karthik kept pointing, looking from the bird to Joseph and back.
“Pigeon,” Joseph said again, slowly.

qa.q: Which floor does Joseph Uncle live on?
qa.a: He lives on the fourth floor.

qa.q: What did Karthik want when he pointed at the ledge and said "Ah!"?
qa.a: He wanted Joseph to look at the pigeon with him; he was interested and excited to share what he saw.

qa.q: What did Joseph do that helps Karthik's language?
qa.a: He looked where Karthik pointed and named the bird, "Pigeon," giving him the word for what he was sharing.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel when Karthik waves and points at him?
qa.a: He probably feels pleased and included, as Karthik chose him to share the moment with.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler waving bye-bye and pointing to share interest, with an adult naming the object he points at.
